analysis.one_liner: Lets Medicare negotiate drug prices directly with manufacturers, fills the coverage gap, and allows cheaper drug imports from Canada.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or a floor vote and died at the end of the 109th Congress with zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would change the Medicare drug benefit in three ways. It would repeal the rule that bars the federal government from negotiating drug prices for Medicare, giving the Health Secretary the same bargaining power the VA and Defense Department already use [S3]. It would eliminate the "donut hole" — the gap in coverage where seniors pay full price for their drugs [S3]. And it would legalize importing lower-priced prescription drugs from Canada, with counterfeit-resistant packaging requirements [S3]. It was referred to two House committees and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries, who would pay less for prescription drugs through government price negotiation and an eliminated coverage gap, plus consumers who could buy imported drugs from Canada [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Medicare beneficiaries and prescription drug consumers

how_it_helps.text: The bill deletes the 'non-interference' provision in Medicare law and directs the Health and Human Services Secretary to negotiate contracts with drug manufacturers, using authority similar to what the VA and Defense Department use when they buy drugs in bulk [S3].
It repeals the 'initial coverage limit' that creates the gap in Medicare drug coverage, so beneficiaries would no longer face a stretch where they pay the full cost of their drugs [S3].

It restores and expands a drug importation law so that individuals — not just pharmacists and wholesalers — could import qualifying prescription drugs, generally from Canada, where prices are lower [S2][S3].
It requires counterfeit-resistant packaging technology on prescription drugs, both to protect consumers from fakes and to address the safety concerns that had been raised against importation [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, whose revenue would be reduced by negotiated Medicare prices, the filled coverage gap, and reimportation competition [S3].

drawbacks.text: Requiring counterfeit-resistant packaging with specific optically variable technologies would add packaging costs for drug makers, and the bill specifies technology standards similar to those used on U.S. currency, which benefits the vendors of that technology [S3].

Drug manufacturers argue that lower negotiated prices and reimportation reduce revenues available for research into new medicines — a trade-off the bill does not address; the CRS summary records no offsetting funding mechanism [S2].

Imported drugs raise safety and counterfeit concerns, which the bill addresses through testing and packaging rules but which skeptics have historically cited as a reason to block importation [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For Medicare beneficiaries, the benefits are large and direct: negotiated prices, no donut hole, and access to cheaper Canadian drugs [S3]. The costs fall almost entirely on the pharmaceutical industry in the form of lower revenue [S3]. The main honest caveats are the possibility of reduced drug-innovation revenue and the safety complexity of importation, which the bill tries to manage with testing and packaging rules rather than eliminate. On balance, the bill is a straightforward transfer of bargaining power from drug makers to consumers and taxpayers.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to two House committees and then to their health subcommittees, where it sat with no hearing, no markup, and no vote, until the Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Representative David Wu introduced the bill on April 13, 2005; no other member cosponsored it [S4][S5].
It was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee on the day of introduction, and within about a week both referrals went to the Subcommittee on Health [S5].

No further action appears in the record: the bill never received a subcommittee or committee vote and never reached the House floor, and it expired when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers kept the ban on Medicare price negotiation, the coverage gap, and importation restrictions intact; seniors kept paying under the same rules.

for.name: Rep. David Wu
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Medicare Prescription Drug Improvement Act on April 13, 2005.

against.name: House committee leadership (Energy and Commerce; Ways and Means)
against.role: Chairs of the committees of referral, who controlled whether the bill got a hearing
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to their health subcommittees, where it received no hearing, no markup, and no vote for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Pharmaceutical manufacturers
against.what_they_did: The industry long opposed Medicare price negotiation and drug reimportation, the two central provisions of this bill.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and the bill had a single Democratic sponsor with no cosponsors, so the record shows only that it drew no support from either party.

industries.note: Medicare price negotiation, elimination of the coverage gap, and legal reimportation would each cut into the prices and sales volumes that sustain drug company revenue. Their gain from the bill dying was the status quo of higher Medicare drug prices [S3].

industries.industry: Prescription drug plan sponsors and pharmacy benefit managers
industries.note: The Part D benefit was built to run through private plans, and the non-interference clause protected their negotiating role; direct government negotiation would have displaced it. Plans would still administer the benefit, but with less pricing power [S3].
Reimportation from Canada would create a legal export channel to American consumers seeking lower prices. Their interest runs with consumers', not against it [S3].

The bill would mandate overt optically variable counterfeit-resistant packaging on prescription drugs, creating a compliance market for that specific technology. Consumers get anti-counterfeit protection; drug makers bear the cost [S3].
